title: Choose your retirement plan structure: Solo 401(k) vs. SEP-IRA vs. SIMPLE IRA
summary: No employer match means no "free money" step — but you have access to higher-limit retirement vehicles than W-2 employees.
detailsHtml:
The three main options

Solo 401(k) (best for most): You can contribute as both employee ($24,500 in 2026) and employer (roughly 20% of net self-employment earnings as a sole proprietor or single-member LLC; 25% of W-2 wages if you pay yourself a salary through an S-corp or C-corp — the 25%-of-W-2 vs ~20%-of-net-SE distinction is the most common Solo 401(k) over-contribution error). Total cap $72,000 in 2026 (+$8,000 standard catch-up, +$11,250 super catch-up at 60–63). Roth option available. Allows Mega Backdoor Roth at most providers. The clear winner for most solo contractors with no employees.

SEP-IRA (simpler but capped): Up to 25% of compensation, $72,000 cap in 2026. No employee contribution side, so the effective contribution at lower incomes is smaller than a Solo 401(k). Simpler paperwork. Best for very high-income contractors who want simplicity over optimization.

SIMPLE IRA (rare for solo contractors): Lower limits for 2026: standard $17,000 + $4,000 catch-up at 50+; super catch-up at 60–63 is $5,250. SECURE 2.0 §117 raises this to $18,100 + $3,850 catch-up for plans of employers with 25 or fewer employees (or 26–100 with the elective 4% non-elective / 4% increased match). Required employer match. Generally only used by small businesses with employees who don't want the complexity of a 401(k); see Business §3.1 for the full match comparison.

Comparison at $100K net SE income (sole prop): Solo 401(k): $24,500 + (~$18,587 employer) = $43,087 SEP-IRA: $18,587 SIMPLE IRA: ~$20,000 Solo 401(k) wins by $24,500 at this income
